question: Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) finds parameters θ that:
options: Maximize the probability of the observed data under the model
Minimize the variance of the predictions
Maximize the prior probability of θ
Match the moments of the data exactly
explanation: MLE picks θ to make the observed data as likely as possible under the model. Adding a prior turns this into MAP; full Bayes integrates over θ.

question: Why do we usually minimize *negative log likelihood* instead of maximizing likelihood directly?
options: Logarithms turn products into sums (numerically stable) and the negative makes it a minimization problem suitable for gradient descent
The two are not equivalent — log-likelihood is fundamentally different
explanation: log() is monotonic so the argmax is the same. Products of many small probabilities underflow; sums of logs don't. Most modern ML losses (cross-entropy, MSE under Gaussian noise) are negative log-likelihoods.

question: A model is *biased* if it consistently over- or under-estimates the true value. *Variance* refers to:
options: How much the model's predictions change across different training sets
The spread of the input data
The width of the loss curve
The squared error of a single prediction
explanation: Bias-variance: bias = systematic error of the average prediction; variance = how predictions wobble across resamples of the training data. Total expected error decomposes into bias² + variance + noise.

question: You want to estimate whether a new model is *significantly* better than a baseline. The right tool is:
options: A hypothesis test (e.g. paired bootstrap, McNemar's test) over many evaluation runs or items
A single side-by-side accuracy comparison on the test set
explanation: A single number can flip on a different sample. Hypothesis tests quantify whether the gap is bigger than the noise. Bootstrap is a robust default when you don't trust normality assumptions.
